newsitem.title: USA: Navistar breaks even in fourth quarter.
newsitem.headline: Navistar breaks even in fourth quarter.

text.p: Navistar International Inc., a major producer of trucks and school buses, said Wednesday it broke even in the fourth quarter as profits were wiped out by a charge to terminate its next-generation truck project.

The Chicago-based company reported no net income for the quarter ended Oct. 31, and a loss of 10 cents per share after the payment of dividends on preferred stock. That compared with profits of $56 million, or 66 cents per share, in the year-ago period. Consolidated sales and revenues fell to $1.5 billion from $1.8 billion.

The results include a $35 million charge to discontinue its $180 million plan, announced in June, to develop next-generation trucks. Navistar made the decision in September because it was unable to resolve issues with the United Auto Workers union.
"While our results can be attributed to a downturn in the industry, our performance last year was not acceptable," said Navistar Chairman John Horne.
"We now are executing strategies to retool those businesses where performance is lacking and to grow those where we're gaining competitive advantages."

Navistar said it expected industry demand for heavy trucks in the United States and Canada will reach 170,000 units in 1997, down 13 percent from the 195,400 heavy trucks sold by the industry in 1996.
Navistar also said it expected industry demand for medium trucks in the United States and Canada will reach 112,000 units in 1997, down slightly from 113,200 in 1996.
Navistar forecast industry demand for school buses in fiscal 1997 will be little changed from the 32,500 buses sold in 1996.

Navistar said it remained the sales leader in the United States and Canadian retail markets for heavy and medium trucks and school buses, with a market share of 27.5 percent, up 0.8 points from a year ago.
Navistar is also a major manufacturer of mid-range diesel engines. Its stock fell 25 cents to $9.375 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-afternoon.
